276.history: The well village of Na Glinn Àrda that keeps the slab laid over the mason's crack, the eldest of the three wells that claim it. In the thousand and seventy-first year a wet spring opened a crack below the slab's stain, and the households laid white stones along it. From the thousand one hundred and twentieth year the families nearest the crack sat the slab in turn through the dark half of every year, a household at a time; Beathan mac Shomhairle sat among the first six, and Gilleonan and Ìde kept their first turn the same winter. The king came up alone once and sat a night among them. In the two thousand four hundred and third year the families chose one keeper by lot, and Oighrig nic Dhòmhnaill drew the white stone; a house was built for her with its door to the slab, and Niocol Snaidhear ground her a stone cup. Gilleasbuig Beag, who drew after her, was rowed to Eilean chrom for a basket of coal, and Giorsal Bhàn laid the coal back under the slab. Somhairle died against the slab in the three thousand and twenty-fifth year and is buried beside it; Diorbhail kept the Line after him. In Catrìona's years the lot was drawn from every part of the hills, the keepers were made nine, and Taigh na Lice became a place walked to for its own sake.
276.known_for: the slab, the lot and Taigh na Lice

2001.history: A harbour of round, turf-roofed houses at the deep-water side of the river mouth below Loch chrom, near enough An Cnoc Ruadh to pay it salt. The first houses were raised in the thousand three hundred and forty-seventh year, where the king's blood had first come down to the sea, and within a season the households were paying their salt to An Cnoc Ruadh rather than keeping it among themselves, with no word sent from Dùn ìseal to start it. An Cnoc Ruadh's list counts them among its holder's households, and the harbour's boats carried salt up the lake to the ford in the autumns.
2001.known_for: the round houses that paid An Cnoc Ruadh salt

45.history: A harbour along the lake shore from An Cnoc Ruadh, where the hill's households drew up their boats in sheds of stone and turf. Within a generation of the first sheds the boats kept there put out oftener than from An Cnoc Ruadh's own strand, and in the four thousand and forty-seventh year it was An Cnoc Ruadh's fishing harbour in all but the reciters' naming. It was never banked or palisaded, trusting to the hill above it. Its boat-sheds were built long and low against the lake's winds, each shed holding two boats, and the households of the hill took turns at the drawing-up after every storm. Its fishers were among the first on the lake to cut the paired tide-marks on their own landing stones.

88.history: A point on the Abhainn fhionn where households from An Cnoc Ruadh's country found an old river landing, its stones set for a boat's keel by hands none living could name, and built their houses about it in the four thousand three hundred and twenty-eighth year. They named the place for what they found, the ancient headland, and used the landing as they found it rather than mend it, as settlers did wherever Seann-Dhaoine' work still stood. The households came down from the lake shore by boat, and the landing took their boats at every state of the river as it had taken Seann-Dhaoine' boats. They kept An Cnoc Ruadh's roll at their fires as their own.
88.known_for: the old landing on the Abhainn fhionn

504.history: A settlement at the edge of Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag, raised by households come down from An Cnoc Ruadh in the middle of the age. They took their timber only from the river's far side and never from the unclaimed wood, and marked the line with a row of unhewn stones. When a boy not yet seven was lost past the stones in the two thousand four hundred and fifty-first year, the settlement and its neighbours searched three days into the wood without one sign of him; Iain of Muileann bhàn, lame from the passes, said aloud that a wood no household would fell was not a wood that gave back what it took, and the searchers stopped at the stones.
504.known_for: the line of stones at the forest's edge

232.history: A settlement founded on the south-western plain in the four thousand three hundred and forty-seventh year, round a house whose walls were limed white. The lime was burned from the shells of Seann-Dhaoine' middens along the coast, which the settlers judged no one's any longer to keep; the households took their name from the house and kept its walls white every spring. It traded cloth and lime along the coast road and sent its people to the ford. The settlers came from the older harbours of the south-west, and the first of them to lime her walls white did so, the telling says, so that her husband could find the house from the sea in the dusk.
